Some tools read a dotenv file rather than the environment, and some only want
one to exist. A project that keeps its secrets in the vault had nothing to give
them.

### Added

- `poo` writes that file from the list `.monkeys` already carries: every
  secret's key alone on a line, every public value as it stands.

  ```sh
  monkeys poo
  ```
  > ```
  > wrote /tmp/monkeys-jn4u9q/.env for @test: 2 keys, 1 value
  > ```
  ```
  # monkeys' poo @test. read https://monk3ys.dev/poo
  DATABASE_URL
  STRIPE_SECRET_KEY
  PORT=3000
  ```

  A key with nothing after it sets nothing, so the file satisfies whatever
  wanted one while the secrets keep arriving through `run`. It lands in `/tmp`,
  so nothing appears in a project that did not ask for it.

  The keys carry no placeholder on purpose. Measured against the three things
  that read such a file, a bare key is the only form safe in all of them:
  dotenv ignores it either way, but Compose's `env_file` takes a bare key from
  the host environment while `KEY=x` sends `x` into the container, and a shell
  that sources the file keeps the real value for a bare key while `KEY=x`
  overwrites it. A placeholder moves the failure from the start of the program
  to the first call that needs the key.

  One file is written, never one per profile, because which profile a program
  runs under is `run`'s decision and a second place to decide it is a second
  place to get it wrong.

### Documentation

- [poo](https://monk3ys.dev/poo), and the landing page and the skill catch up
  with `pack`.
